title: Plant Anatomy
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Plant Anatomy curriculum: plant cell wall, meristems, simple and complex tissues, tissue systems, and internal (anatomical) structure of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf, including secondary growth.

questions.question: The primary cell wall of a young plant cell is composed mainly of:
options: Cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin
Lignin only
Suberin and cutin
Chitin
questions.correct_answer: Cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin
questions.explanation: The primary wall is thin and flexible, built from cellulose microfibrils held in a hemicellulose-pectin matrix, allowing cell expansion during growth.

questions.question: The middle lamella, located between adjacent plant cell walls, is composed chiefly of:
options: Calcium and magnesium pectates
Cellulose
Lignin
Suberin
questions.correct_answer: Calcium and magnesium pectates
questions.explanation: The middle lamella is a pectin-rich layer that cements adjoining cell walls together; it is formed first during cell plate formation.

questions.question: Plasmodesmata are important because they:
options: Provide cytoplasmic connections between adjacent cells through the cell wall
Strengthen the secondary wall
Regulate stomatal opening
Form the boundary of the vacuole
questions.correct_answer: Provide cytoplasmic connections between adjacent cells through the cell wall
questions.explanation: Plasmodesmata are narrow cytoplasmic channels that traverse cell walls, allowing communication and transport of substances between neighbouring cells (forming the symplast).

questions.question: Meristematic tissue is characterised by:
options: Small, thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm and high mitotic activity
Large, dead cells with lignified walls
Cells with large vacuoles and no nucleus
Cells specialised for long-distance water conduction
questions.correct_answer: Small, thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm and high mitotic activity
questions.explanation: Meristematic cells are undifferentiated, isodiametric, thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm, prominent nuclei and active cell division, giving rise to permanent tissues.

questions.question: Apical meristems are located at:
options: The tips of roots and shoots
The nodes only
Beneath the epidermis throughout the stem
The centre of mature secondary xylem
questions.correct_answer: The tips of roots and shoots
questions.explanation: Apical meristems occur at root and shoot tips and are responsible for primary growth, increasing the length of the plant body.

questions.question: The vascular cambium and cork cambium are examples of:
options: Lateral meristems responsible for secondary growth
Apical meristems responsible for primary growth
Intercalary meristems found at internodes
Ground meristem giving rise to pith
questions.correct_answer: Lateral meristems responsible for secondary growth
questions.explanation: Lateral meristems form cylinders running along the long axis of roots and stems and produce secondary tissues that increase girth.

questions.question: Intercalary meristems, found at the base of internodes in grasses, are responsible for:
options: Rapid regrowth of leaves and stems after grazing or mowing
Secondary thickening of the stem
Root hair formation
Wound healing at the cambium
questions.correct_answer: Rapid regrowth of leaves and stems after grazing or mowing
questions.explanation: Intercalary meristems persist at internode/leaf bases in grasses, allowing continued elongation even after the tip is removed by grazing.

questions.question: Parenchyma cells are best described as:
options: Living, thin-walled, relatively unspecialised cells often involved in photosynthesis or storage
Dead cells with thick lignified walls for support
Elongated cells with tapering ends for mechanical strength
Cells specialised exclusively for water conduction
questions.correct_answer: Living, thin-walled, relatively unspecialised cells often involved in photosynthesis or storage
questions.explanation: Parenchyma are the most common, least specialised plant cells, typically living at maturity with thin primary walls, functioning in photosynthesis, storage and healing.

questions.question: Collenchyma tissue provides mechanical support in young, growing organs mainly because:
options: Its cells have unevenly thickened, non-lignified primary walls that remain flexible
Its cells are dead with uniformly thickened lignified walls
It consists of vessel elements
It contains chloroplasts for photosynthesis only
questions.correct_answer: Its cells have unevenly thickened, non-lignified primary walls that remain flexible
questions.explanation: Collenchyma cells are living with unevenly thickened (often at the corners) primary walls of cellulose and pectin, giving flexible support to still-growing organs.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma differs from collenchyma chiefly in that sclerenchyma cells:
options: Are dead at maturity with uniformly thickened, lignified walls
Remain alive and continue to grow
Have unevenly thickened primary walls only
Function mainly in food storage
questions.correct_answer: Are dead at maturity with uniformly thickened, lignified walls
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma cells develop thick, lignified secondary walls and lose their protoplast at maturity, providing rigid, permanent mechanical support.

questions.question: The two main types of sclerenchyma cells are:
options: Fibres and sclereids
Vessels and tracheids
Sieve tubes and companion cells
Guard cells and subsidiary cells
questions.correct_answer: Fibres and sclereids
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma comprises elongated fibres, which occur in strands or sheaths, and sclereids (stone cells), which are variable in shape and often found in fruit flesh or seed coats.

questions.question: Xylem functions primarily in:
options: Conduction of water and dissolved minerals, and providing mechanical support
Conduction of manufactured food (photosynthates)
Gas exchange
Storage of starch only
questions.correct_answer: Conduction of water and dissolved minerals, and providing mechanical support
questions.explanation: Xylem tissue conducts water and minerals from roots to aerial parts and, being lignified, also provides structural support to the plant.

questions.question: The conducting elements of xylem are tracheids and vessel elements; vessel elements are distinguished by:
options: Perforation plates connecting cells end-to-end into a continuous tube
Being living cells with dense cytoplasm
Lacking lignified walls
Conducting food rather than water
questions.correct_answer: Perforation plates connecting cells end-to-end into a continuous tube
questions.explanation: Vessel elements have perforated end walls that join to form long continuous vessels, allowing more efficient water flow than the imperforate tracheids.

questions.question: Phloem transports mainly:
options: Organic solutes (photosynthates) such as sucrose from source to sink tissues
Water and mineral salts from root to shoot
Oxygen for respiration
Auxins exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Organic solutes (photosynthates) such as sucrose from source to sink tissues
questions.explanation: Phloem is responsible for translocation of organic food materials, chiefly sucrose, produced in photosynthetic source tissues to non-photosynthetic sink tissues.

questions.question: Sieve tube elements are able to conduct food efficiently despite lacking a nucleus at maturity because:
options: Adjacent companion cells retain nuclei and metabolically support them
They contain chloroplasts that generate ATP
They are surrounded by lignified fibres
They possess perforation plates like vessels
questions.correct_answer: Adjacent companion cells retain nuclei and metabolically support them
questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements lose their nucleus at maturity but remain alive; the closely connected companion cells, rich in organelles, carry out metabolic functions for them.

questions.question: Sieve plates are found at the end walls of sieve tube elements and function to:
options: Allow passage of phloem sap between successive sieve tube elements via sieve pores
Prevent any movement of solutes between cells
Conduct water upward from roots
Store starch grains permanently
questions.correct_answer: Allow passage of phloem sap between successive sieve tube elements via sieve pores
questions.explanation: Sieve plates are perforated end walls with sieve pores lined by callose, through which phloem sap flows from one sieve element to the next.

questions.question: The three fundamental tissue systems found in the plant body are:
options: Dermal, ground (fundamental) and vascular
Epidermal, cortical and pith
Xylem, phloem and cambium
Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma
questions.correct_answer: Dermal, ground (fundamental) and vascular
questions.explanation: All plant organs are built from three tissue systems: the dermal system (epidermis), the ground/fundamental system (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma), and the vascular system (xylem and phloem).

questions.question: The epidermis, as part of the dermal tissue system, commonly bears which protective covering?
options: A waxy cuticle
A layer of lignin
A layer of suberin only in leaves
Chloroplasts in guard-cell-free zones only
questions.correct_answer: A waxy cuticle
questions.explanation: The epidermis of aerial parts secretes a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss and offers some protection against pathogens.

questions.question: Stomata regulate:
options: Gaseous exchange and transpiration through pores flanked by guard cells
Uptake of water by root hairs
Translocation of sugars in phloem
Secondary thickening of the stem
questions.correct_answer: Gaseous exchange and transpiration through pores flanked by guard cells
questions.explanation: Stomata are epidermal pores bordered by two guard cells whose turgor changes open or close the pore, controlling gas exchange and water vapour loss.

questions.question: In a typical dicotyledonous root in transverse section, the vascular tissue is arranged as:
options: A central solid core with xylem arms alternating with phloem strands (radial arrangement)
Scattered vascular bundles throughout the ground tissue
A single ring of collateral bundles surrounding a large pith
Xylem and phloem forming a continuous cylinder with no pith
questions.correct_answer: A central solid core with xylem arms alternating with phloem strands (radial arrangement)
questions.explanation: Dicot roots show a radial vascular arrangement with star-shaped xylem at the centre and phloem patches located between the xylem arms, usually with no or a small pith.

questions.question: The endodermis of a root is anatomically distinguished by the presence of:
options: Casparian strips (bands) in the radial and transverse walls
Chloroplasts in every cell
A thick waxy cuticle
Large intercellular air spaces
questions.correct_answer: Casparian strips (bands) in the radial and transverse walls
questions.explanation: The endodermis contains suberised Casparian strips that block the apoplastic pathway, forcing water and solutes to cross the plasma membrane (symplastic route) to enter the stele.

questions.question: The pericycle in a root is significant because it:
options: Gives rise to lateral roots and contributes to the vascular cambium during secondary growth
Forms the outermost protective layer
Is the site of stomatal formation
Conducts water directly to the xylem
questions.correct_answer: Gives rise to lateral roots and contributes to the vascular cambium during secondary growth
questions.explanation: The pericycle is a meristematic layer just inside the endodermis that initiates lateral roots and, in many dicots, participates in forming the vascular cambium.

questions.question: A key anatomical difference between a monocot root and a dicot root is that the monocot root typically has:
options: A large parenchymatous pith with numerous xylem and phloem groups arranged around it
No pith and a solid star-shaped xylem core
Secondary growth from a vascular cambium
Xylem restricted to two poles only
questions.correct_answer: A large parenchymatous pith with numerous xylem and phloem groups arranged around it
questions.explanation: Monocot roots are usually polyarch with numerous xylem and phloem bundles arranged around a well-developed central pith, and normally lack secondary growth.

questions.question: In a typical herbaceous dicotyledonous stem, vascular bundles are arranged:
options: In a single ring around a central pith
Scattered irregularly throughout the ground tissue
As a solid radial core like the root
In two concentric rings of equal size
questions.correct_answer: In a single ring around a central pith
questions.explanation: Dicot stems typically show a single ring of collateral vascular bundles surrounding a central pith, with cortex outside the ring.

questions.question: In a typical monocotyledonous stem (e.g., maize), the vascular bundles are:
options: Scattered throughout the ground tissue with no clear ring arrangement
Arranged in a single peripheral ring only
Absent, replaced by diffuse xylem cells
Confined to the centre of the stem only
questions.correct_answer: Scattered throughout the ground tissue with no clear ring arrangement
questions.explanation: Monocot stems lack a clear cortex-pith distinction because their numerous collateral vascular bundles are scattered throughout the ground tissue.

questions.question: A collateral vascular bundle, typical of dicot and monocot stems, has:
options: Xylem and phloem located on the same radius, with phloem usually outside xylem
Phloem completely surrounding the xylem
Xylem surrounding the phloem on all sides
Xylem and phloem on opposite radii of the bundle
questions.correct_answer: Xylem and phloem located on the same radius, with phloem usually outside xylem
questions.explanation: In collateral bundles, xylem and phloem lie side by side on the same radius, with phloem typically situated toward the outside of the xylem.

questions.question: A bundle sheath surrounding a vascular bundle in a monocot stem functions to:
options: Provide mechanical protection and, in leaves, aid in photosynthesis (e.g., in C4 plants)
Conduct water exclusively
Replace the function of the epidermis
Produce secondary xylem
questions.correct_answer: Provide mechanical protection and, in leaves, aid in photosynthesis (e.g., in C4 plants)
questions.explanation: The bundle sheath, often sclerenchymatous, encloses and protects the vascular bundle; in C4 leaf anatomy (Kranz anatomy) it also plays a key photosynthetic role.

questions.question: Secondary growth in a dicot stem results from the activity of the:
options: Vascular cambium and cork cambium (phellogen)
Apical meristem alone
Pericycle only
Endodermis
questions.correct_answer: Vascular cambium and cork cambium (phellogen)
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium produces secondary xylem and phloem, while the phellogen produces the periderm (cork), together increasing the girth of the stem.

questions.question: Annual growth rings visible in the secondary xylem of temperate trees result from:
options: Seasonal variation in the size and wall thickness of xylem cells produced by the cambium
Alternating layers of phloem and cortex
Deposition of suberin at regular intervals
Periodic activity of the apical meristem
questions.correct_answer: Seasonal variation in the size and wall thickness of xylem cells produced by the cambium
questions.explanation: Springwood (earlywood) cells are larger and thinner-walled while summerwood (latewood) cells are smaller and thicker-walled, and the boundary between one year's latewood and the next year's earlywood appears as a visible ring.

questions.question: The cork cambium (phellogen) produces cork (phellem) cells that are impermeable to water mainly due to deposition of:
options: Suberin
Lignin
Cellulose
Pectin
questions.correct_answer: Suberin
questions.explanation: Phellem cells have walls impregnated with suberin, a waxy, waterproof substance that protects the stem after the epidermis is sloughed off.

questions.question: Lenticels, found on the surface of woody stems, function to allow:
options: Gaseous exchange through the otherwise impermeable periderm
Absorption of water directly into the phloem
Attachment of leaves to the stem
Movement of sugars to the roots
questions.correct_answer: Gaseous exchange through the otherwise impermeable periderm
questions.explanation: Lenticels are loosely packed regions of the periderm that permit oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange between internal tissues and the atmosphere once the epidermis is replaced by cork.

questions.question: In a dorsiventral dicot leaf, the palisade mesophyll is located:
options: Just beneath the upper (adaxial) epidermis
Just beneath the lower (abaxial) epidermis
In the midrib only
Surrounding the vascular bundles exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Just beneath the upper (adaxial) epidermis
questions.explanation: Palisade mesophyll consists of elongated, closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells located toward the upper surface where light intensity is greatest, maximising photosynthesis.

questions.question: Spongy mesophyll, found toward the lower surface of a dorsiventral leaf, is characterised by:
options: Loosely arranged, irregularly shaped cells with large intercellular air spaces
Tightly packed columnar cells with few air spaces
Cells lacking chloroplasts entirely
Lignified cells providing mechanical support
questions.correct_answer: Loosely arranged, irregularly shaped cells with large intercellular air spaces
questions.explanation: Spongy mesophyll cells are loosely packed with extensive intercellular spaces that facilitate gas diffusion between stomata and photosynthetic cells.

questions.question: A key anatomical difference in most monocot (isobilateral) leaves compared to dicot leaves is that monocot leaves typically:
options: Lack differentiation into palisade and spongy mesophyll, appearing similar on both surfaces
Have stomata only on the upper surface
Lack vascular bundles entirely
Have a thicker cuticle on the lower surface only
questions.correct_answer: Lack differentiation into palisade and spongy mesophyll, appearing similar on both surfaces
questions.explanation: Many monocot leaves are isobilateral, with undifferentiated mesophyll and stomata on both surfaces, unlike the dorsiventral dicot leaf.

questions.question: Kranz anatomy, found in the leaves of C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane, is characterised by:
options: A conspicuous bundle sheath of large chloroplast-containing cells tightly encircling each vascular bundle
Complete absence of mesophyll tissue
Vascular bundles located only at the leaf margins
Stomata confined to the midrib region
questions.correct_answer: A conspicuous bundle sheath of large chloroplast-containing cells tightly encircling each vascular bundle
questions.explanation: Kranz ('wreath') anatomy features a prominent bundle sheath with large, chloroplast-rich cells surrounding the vascular bundle, functionally separating CO2 fixation (mesophyll) from the Calvin cycle (bundle sheath) in C4 photosynthesis.

questions.question: Anomalous (unusual) secondary growth, seen in stems such as Bougainvillea, typically results from:
options: Successive rings of cambium forming outside the normal vascular cylinder
Complete absence of any cambial activity
Only primary growth occurring throughout the plant's life
Formation of vascular tissue exclusively in the root
questions.correct_answer: Successive rings of cambium forming outside the normal vascular cylinder
questions.explanation: In anomalous secondary growth, additional cambial rings arise outside the first, producing concentric rings of vascular tissue embedded in conjunctive parenchyma.

questions.question: Laticifers, found in plants such as Hevea (rubber) and Papaya, are specialised secretory structures that:
options: Contain and conduct latex, a milky fluid of varied composition
Store only crystals of calcium oxalate
Function exclusively in water conduction
Are modified stomata
questions.correct_answer: Contain and conduct latex, a milky fluid of varied composition
questions.explanation: Laticifers are specialised cells or cell series containing latex, which may contain rubber, alkaloids, or other compounds, and often play a role in defence.

questions.question: Resin ducts (canals), found in conifers, are formed by:
options: Schizogenous separation of cells that secrete resin into the resulting intercellular space
Lysigenous breakdown of a single large cell
Fusion of xylem vessels
Modification of guard cells
questions.correct_answer: Schizogenous separation of cells that secrete resin into the resulting intercellular space
questions.explanation: Resin ducts arise schizogenously, where surrounding epithelial cells actively secrete resin into a canal formed by the separation of cells, rather than by cell breakdown (lysigeny).
